content: 1. When developing AI technologies, it is essential to identify and adhere to evolving regulatory requirements. These frameworks often address data protection, security, and privacy, while also incorporating emerging principles such as equitable access and the preservation of human autonomy. Compliance measures must be integrated into the development and updates of the technology. 2. Developers must ensure adherence to country-specific or regional export rules and guidelines, such as the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Singapore’s Personal Data Protection Act, or the US Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). For example, GDPR Article 22 prohibits individuals from being subjected solely to automated decision-making processes with significant effects. 3. It is critical to define open norms and concepts that can be justified to affected parties and experts with relevant knowledge of the AI application. 4. Establishing robust data management plans is crucial. These plans should include clear guidelines for data collection, storage, organization, and access to ensure data security, privacy, and confidentiality. 5. Developers must understand the data collection and sharing requirements and regulations in the countries, sectors, and institutions of potential users. This includes legal requirements for managing consent for the use of training data. 6. The type of data being collected, as well as its storage location and method, must be determined. Physical infrastructure and operational processes should be assessed to ensure data security and integrity. 7. Confidentiality and privacy protections must be clearly defined for different contexts. Guidelines and protocols should be established for the proper collection, storage, organization, access, and use of personal, proprietary, and public data. 8. The duration of data storage, conditions for data sharing, and other temporal considerations must be determined. Anonymized data should be prioritized whenever possible. 9. Responsibility for data governance must be clearly assigned, and appropriate follow-up measures should be ensured. All groups with access to the data throughout the product’s lifecycle must be identified, and any secondary uses of the data must be explicitly determined. 10. AI technologies should comply with established international, regional, or national standards and performance benchmarks. Examples include ISO standards for security and privacy, the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) guidelines, IEEE 7000 series for privacy and fairness, and Health Level 7 (HL7) standards for administrative and clinical health data transfer. 11. During deployment and maintenance, it is essential to engage and educate multiple stakeholders, ensuring inclusivity to better understand their needs and develop tailored solutions. Responsibilities for actions, timelines, and methods must be clearly delineated. 12. Proposed approaches should be designed, discussed, and validated with stakeholders, including policymakers, project leaders, solution engineers, potential users, domain experts, and ethics and privacy specialists. 13. Stakeholders should be trained on the objectives, functions, features, and usage scenarios of the AI tool. Continuous engagement and user support are necessary. 14. The performance and impact of AI technologies on healthcare must be formally evaluated. Continuous improvement of the design and development should align with ethical principles, governance guidelines, and applicable legal obligations. 15. Risks associated with the technology and its intended use in various healthcare settings should be regularly assessed to manage deployment, development, and maintenance. 16. Ministries of health should evaluate whether AI technologies are appropriate and necessary, ensuring they contribute to universal health coverage without diverting resources from proven but underfunded interventions. 17. AI technologies must undergo rigorous testing, monitoring, and evaluation, including clinical trials, to identify and address any unanticipated hazards or consequences. Regulatory agencies should support transparent communication of outcomes and performance monitoring. 18. Countries must have sufficient regulatory capacity to scrutinize AI technologies used in healthcare. For low-risk AI technologies, regulators may consider lighter premarket scrutiny. Prospective testing in randomized trials is preferred over reliance on existing laboratory datasets. 19. Liability rules must be adapted to address accountability for negative consequences arising from AI use. This includes product liability, personal liability of decision-makers, input liability, and liability to data donors. Mechanisms for assigning vicarious liability should also be established. 20. Legal systems must guarantee redress for undue damage caused by AI technologies. Independent oversight should ensure equitable access to quality healthcare. 21. Ministries of health must prepare for the introduction and use of AI technologies by ensuring institutional readiness and technical capacity. This includes training government officials to evaluate AI technologies based on ethical principles and involving healthcare authorities and medical professionals in AI design and software engineering. 22. Civil society, medical staff, and patient groups should be consulted during the introduction of AI technologies and included in external audits and monitoring of their functioning. Investments in health systems should accompany AI technology deployment to capture its benefits effectively. 23. Proper infrastructure is a prerequisite for deploying AI in healthcare systems. Criteria should be established to identify and measure infrastructure requirements, and when necessary, infrastructure should be strengthened with civil society support and international cooperation. 24. Ministries of health should identify effective alternatives if infrastructure is lacking, the AI technology is too expensive, or it poses a high risk to patients. 25. High-quality data is essential to prevent unintended harm from AI systems. Poor-quality or inaccurate data can lead to biased inferences, misleading analyses, and poorly designed health applications. 26. Health data management must protect patient privacy and confidentiality while adhering to rules for data sharing. Data processing should be regulated for representativeness, accuracy, harmonization, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability, with informed consent from data providers. 27. Access to and use of data from digital self-care applications and wearable technologies should be regulated. Data collection, storage, and use must align with principles of data minimization. 28. Patients and consumers who provide data should have access to and be allowed to reuse their data. Their data should not be monopolized by AI technology providers. 29. Quality control measures should ensure data representativeness across different population groups. Mechanisms and procedures should be in place to collect relevant patient data for training AI technologies according to the specific environment, culture, and community. 30. Patients and consumers should be informed about the data used to train AI systems. 31. AI technologies for health should enhance human decision-making and empower medical professionals rather than replace them. Human judgment should be applied to disease predictions and treatment recommendations made by AI. 32. Ministries of health should specify the types of information clinicians need to make independent judgments about AI results or outcomes. Patients should receive clear, meaningful information to make informed decisions about health recommendations based on AI technology. 33. The use of AI predictive analytics in healthcare raises ethical concerns regarding informed consent and individual autonomy. The necessity of the AI technology should be assessed, and patients should have the right to refuse its use. 34. Health data processing must respect the right to privacy and ensure patients maintain control over decisions, including their informed consent. Up-to-date data protection and confidentiality laws should be a prerequisite for AI use. 35. Independent oversight and other forms of redress should be available to protect patient privacy and data confidentiality. Data protection supervisory agencies must have sufficient resources for effective privacy protection. 36. Ministries of health should employ experts to evaluate whether AI tools meet privacy standards, fostering trust among patients who provide data. Protocols for collecting, storing, and sharing personal data must be established.
